This is one of the most interesting issues facing autonomous vehicles. I brought it up recently in a thread on that other site, but came at it from the opposite angle: with the current state of technology, autonomous vehicles cannot make those decisions. A human driver can see a person lying in the grass by the side of the road, distinguish between a school bus and a panel truck, and see whether a minivan is filled with kids or plumbing supplies. The technology to enable a self-driving car to make those distinctions in a split second is not practical today and will not be for many years. If flips the ethical question around a bit: do we want these vehicles on the road, knowing they are not equipped to make those decisions at all?

Self driving cars would be able to make these decisions very easily if all the cars on the road published their position and occupancy stats. Since that information is necessary for optimal traffic control, providing it will most likely be a standard feature once self-driving becomes the norm.

Personally I think this point is moot and overplayed.

Algorithms which are complex enough to accurately predict the chance of survival of all participants in a crash are quite a way off. The first generation of self-driving cars will likely just have harm-minimisation strategies (e.g. 'Avoid as many cars as possible while coming to a stop as soon as possible'). At most it will pick the safest of the available options for the car, as they are unlikely to have sufficient complexity to be able to predict the actions of other cars in a crash situation.

When 100% of cars are self driving a crash would only occur in the chance of a system error and redundancy can be built in to avoid this. In case of a crash I see there being 3 main options:

  1. In chance of error and likely crash all cars in the affected area go into an 'emergency stop' mode where they reduce speed as quickly as possible, taking into account the stopping distances of other cars.
  2. Each car calculates the survival probability of each participant and creates its own strategy on how to reduce fatalities across the whole accident. This would have to be constantly re-calculated to account for the strategies other cars have chosen.
  3. The cars communicate and somehow come up with a collaborative harm-reduction strategy to reduce fatalities.

The problem with options 2 & 3 is that they are far more complex (especially if some cars are already in an error-state) and prone to failure. On paper it brings up interesting philosophical questions, but in reality I just don't think it will be a big issue in reality for a long time.

I agree with your analysis. I'll go further and say the number of deaths caused by driving accidents will be lower in the future.
